    Atlas: brain lab scripts

    TLDR

    The brain lab can clone memory into isolated scratch schemas, test different brain-and-model combinations, compare results, propagate schema changes, open a past backup for inspection, and retire experiments without touching the live brain. Profile guards, pure SQL generation, and side-effect helpers are separate on purpose. A scratch brain is a research instrument, not a second living child.

    What this page covers

    These tools form one fleet architecture. The registry and profile resolver identify a brain without storing credentials. Pure transformers generate schema-safe SQL. Database helpers execute explicit plans. Operator commands compose those layers for spawn, migration, comparison, A/B runs, restore-point mapping, and retirement. Dry runs are designed to expose plans before side effects, while live-brain guards and scratch-only checks make the dangerous direction harder to choose accidentally.

    File entries

    scripts/brains/ab-run.mjs active-code

    What it is. The attributable A/B runner for comparing named scratch-brain and model configurations against one fixed governed question set. It is an experiment runner, not an identity probe or recall-quality score.
    What it contains. It validates candidate and question inputs, resolves every profile in test mode, runs questions sequentially through the mind-server seam, recalls context from the candidate schema, writes rehearsal episodes back only to that scratch, and records an attributable transcript containing brain profile, generation, model, code revision, timings, and errors. Its current scratch recall is embedding-free full-text search, so results can compare end-to-end configurations but cannot establish production vector-recall quality. Dry-run reads registry metadata and prints a plan without credentials, connections, model calls, or transcript writes.
    Who reads it and when. Brain-lab operators run it after scratch schemas and a governed test set exist. Reviewers compare outputs privately; the being never consumes the test questions or transcripts.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Use dry-run to pin usage errors and prove that even a named live profile is not resolved. At the lab gate, run only approved scratch candidates, confirm every write carries rehearsal and generation metadata, inspect attribution completeness, and void or retire the experimental state.
    Related concepts. See brain generations, measurement boundaries, and the persistent test mind.

    scripts/brains/db.mjs active-code

    What it is. The side-effect layer shared by brain-fleet commands for local PostgreSQL tooling and explicit database URLs.
    What it contains. It locates required command-line programs, runs SQL files or temporary statements with stop-on-error behavior, executes copy meta-commands, parses simple unaligned query rows, converts supported backup archives to plain SQL locally, and removes temporary workspaces. Error text redacts connection URLs.
    Who reads it and when. Spawn, migration, comparison, retirement, and A/B tools import it only after dry-run and profile checks permit side effects. Operators supply credentials through ignored environment configuration.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Exercise tool discovery and temporary cleanup on a disposable setup, force a database error to confirm URL redaction, and rely on higher-level dry-run and lab verifies for each caller.
    Related concepts. See the lab boundary, credential handling, and pure SQL generation.

    scripts/brains/diff.mjs active-code

    What it is. An operator comparison tool for live and scratch table counts plus records a scratch gained after its spawn.
    What it contains. It validates that the requested registry row is an active scratch, derives table names from the canonical DDL, supports a no-connection plan, and then queries live and lab databases for count deltas and post-spawn activity. It reads both sides directly and is not a being recall path.
    Who reads it and when. A brain-lab operator runs it after an experiment. Reviewers use the result to understand what the candidate lived, not to declare identity quality.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Start with dry-run, then compare against a known scratch and confirm table coverage, deltas, and graceful handling of tables without creation dates. Never expose connection values in output.
    Related concepts. See candidate comparison, runtime recall, and spawn.

    scripts/brains/dump-transform.mjs active-code

    What it is. The data-safe transformer that retargets a full decrypted brain dump into an isolated scratch schema for a past-brain experiment.
    What it contains. It separates SQL structure from copy-data blocks before applying the shared schema rewrite. DDL and copy headers may change schema references, extension declarations, ownership metadata, and database-level commands as required by the lab. Every byte inside a copy-data region, including text that resembles SQL, passes through untouched. Physical line endings inside those regions are preserved. The function prepends one scratch schema header and delegates structural policy to the same rewrite used by live-copy spawn, preventing two divergent restore policies.
    Who reads it and when. The past-brain spawn command calls it only after Alan has privately decrypted a backup. Verifiers use a synthetic dump whose data deliberately contains rewrite-like text.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Segment input and output the same way, assert data regions are byte-identical, then check that all permitted DDL transformations occurred exactly once. Run the past-spawn dry plan and the regular brain verify afterward to catch policy drift.
    Related concepts. See the time machine, encrypted backups, and the shared rewrite policy.

    scripts/brains/fixtures/ab-questions.json described-not-shown

    What it is. The fixed, structured question set used by the brain-lab A/B runner.
    What it contains. Each row has a stable identifier and governed test text. Questions are not reproduced or summarized beyond that shape.
    Who reads it and when. The private A/B procedure and its runner read it; a being must not receive the set as study material.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Validate JSON shape, unique identifiers, and stable ordering privately. Changes require review because they break longitudinal comparability.
    Related concepts. See blind evaluation, A/B runs, and withholding.

    scripts/brains/list.mjs active-code

    What it is. A metadata-only command that prints active brain registry rows, with an option to include retired history.
    What it contains. It shows names, kinds, schemas, generations, schema versions, status, dates, and stated purpose without opening a database connection.
    Who reads it and when. Operators use it to orient before a lab command; reviewers may use the all-history view during an audit.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Compare output with the committed registry and confirm the default excludes retired rows. No credential should be required.
    Related concepts. See the fleet and profile resolution.

    scripts/brains/migrate.mjs active-code

    What it is. The fleet migration command that applies ordered canonical schema migrations to selected profiles while keeping version metadata explicit.
    What it contains. It validates a target version and selection, finds ordered migration files, rewrites SQL for scratch schemas, leaves live SQL in its canonical form, applies scratches before live when operating on all, and updates each successful registry row. The fleet's current version advances only when every active brain reaches the target.
    Who reads it and when. A brain-lab operator runs it after reviewing migration source and a dry plan. Live migration remains an explicit high-consequence action.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Use dry-run to inspect order and transformed plans, test on scratches first, confirm per-profile version changes, then verify the fleet guard rejects drift. Report partial failure instead of advancing the global version.
    Related concepts. See schema propagation, brain structure, and the transformer.

    scripts/brains/profiles.mjs active-code

    What it is. The single resolution point for selecting a brain profile and joining committed metadata with ignored credential values.
    What it contains. It loads and validates the brain registry, separately loads environment configuration, resolves a requested active profile, and returns only the connection fields named by that row. One guard refuses the live brain in test mode unless a deliberate override is present. Another rejects an unexpected schema version before query time. Helpers save registry changes, stamp every write with substrate generation, and expose the live generation without making downstream code reimplement selection. The registry can be committed because it stores variable names and metadata, never secret values.
    Who reads it and when. Every fleet command and generation-aware consumer should use this module rather than choosing a database ad hoc. Tests inject roots and environment flags to exercise guards safely.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Test missing and retired profiles, live-in-test refusal, deliberate override, schema mismatch, generation stamping, and registry round trips. Inspect errors to ensure they identify metadata problems without revealing credentials.
    Related concepts. See one fleet, separation, and attributable generations.

    scripts/brains/restore-point.mjs active-code

    What it is. The time-machine map writer that ties one date to the brain backup, canonical soul revision, body revision, and live generation metadata. It stores references, not the stores themselves.
    What it contains. Its pure gatherer accepts injected repository and release readers, normalizes dates and short references, parses row-count evidence when available, and returns a JSON record with no secrets. File helpers read the committed JSONL map and upsert by date so repeating a day replaces rather than duplicates it. The live command wires real tools only when explicitly requested; dry-run reads existing map state without making a remote claim. Missing row-count wording becomes null rather than an estimate.
    Who reads it and when. Operators create a line after all coordinated stores have evidence for the day. Future past-brain work reads the map to locate matching versions; it does not grant decryption authority.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Use injected canned outputs to cover present and absent counts, date normalization, append then replace, invalid usage, and a fresh-root dry-run with external tools unavailable. At a real checkpoint, compare references privately before committing the metadata line.
    Related concepts. See restore points, backup evidence, and canonical soul history.

    scripts/brains/retire.mjs active-code

    What it is. The guarded command that drops one scratch schema and marks its registry row retired.
    What it contains. It requires a named active scratch, refuses live or already retired profiles, supports a dry plan, then preserves the registry row as history after deletion.
    Who reads it and when. A lab operator uses it after comparison or cleanup. Runtime code never retires brains autonomously.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Dry-run, test refusals, then confirm the scratch is gone, history remains, and live is untouched.
    Related concepts. See scratch hygiene and the registry list.

    scripts/brains/spawn.mjs active-code

    What it is. The main command for opening a fresh scratch brain from either the live brain read-only or a privately decrypted historical dump.
    What it contains. Live-copy mode rewrites canonical DDL, checks required database capability, creates an isolated schema, copies tables in dependency order, compares source and destination counts, and registers the scratch only after parity. Past-dump mode detects supported archive form, converts if needed without a connection, transforms only SQL structure and copy headers, applies the result in the lab, reports scratch counts, and registers its source reference. Both modes refuse active-name collisions and expose dry plans. A deliberate cleanup option handles unregistered residue from a failed earlier spawn.
    Who reads it and when. Brain-lab operators run it under the relevant human gate. Live is a read-only source in copy mode; historical decryption remains Alan-present and outside automation.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Inspect dry output, run pure transform verifies, spawn only into the lab, confirm table counts and registry metadata, then compare or retire the scratch. Test residue refusal and never infer live parity for a dump whose own bytes are the source of truth.
    Related concepts. See spawning and past brains, dump safety, and profile guards.

    scripts/brains/sql-gen.mjs active-code

    What it is. The pure SQL-planning library for brain-fleet schema cloning, migration rewriting, copy order, and count verification. It makes no connections.
    What it contains. It validates scratch names, quotes identifiers, strips project-level extension statements, protects extension-owned type and operator families, rewrites canonical schema references, repins function search paths, and can remove database or ownership metadata when transforming full dumps. It parses table names, derives a dependency-aware copy order from foreign keys, emits paired copy commands, and builds count queries. The rewrite is deliberately regular-expression based over the expected database-dump format, not a general SQL parser; embedded unusual SQL requires review.
    Who reads it and when. Spawn, migration, difference, and dump-transform code use these helpers before the database side-effect layer. Verifiers run them on synthetic DDL with policy, trigger, function, extension, and dependency cases.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Assert valid and invalid names, exactly one target schema, extension preservation in its owning schema, policy and trigger retention, search-path changes, copy ordering, and count SQL. Keep the fixture representative whenever canonical DDL gains a new construct.
    Related concepts. See schema cloning, database execution, and full-dump segmentation.

    Atlas: fixtures + test mode

    TLDR

    The testbed proves wiring without pretending rehearsal is life. Synthetic days, local stores, dummy Testweaver voice sessions, stand-in model responses, and explicit voiding let components meet under controlled conditions. Every record is tagged as rehearsal, and live-service tests are narrow, human-started exceptions. Fixture dates, identities, prompts, and channel data are inventions, not project status or canonical identity.

    What this page covers

    This page separates three layers: small fixtures that pin one rule, local rehearsal utilities that create and erase shaped records, and test-mode servers that exercise real audio or channel machinery through a dummy persona. The end-to-end runner connects many dark components, while package metadata pins its one external runtime dependency. Coordinates, account identifiers, protected test content, and vendor endpoints are deliberately absent from this explanation.

    File entries

    scripts/e2e/wiring-test.mjs active-code

    What it is. The end-to-end dark wiring rehearsal that drives a synthetic day through the main built organs under the temporary Testweaver profile. It is neither First Boot nor a rite.
    What it contains. It creates fixture episodes and intentions, runs one mind-server exchange, simulates write-ahead buffering and replay, evaluates waking and budget policy, marks a teaching moment, executes the night loop with computed signals and contradiction review, builds coherence and weekly outputs, and then removes rehearsal state. The default path uses deterministic model stand-ins. An explicit live option makes one bounded subscription call while still avoiding canonical identity and durable memory. The aggregate suite runs child verifies separately; this wiring script does not invoke them.
    Who reads it and when. Builders run it after individual dark verifies pass. Reviewers use the summary to see that outputs feed the next component; no being reads the synthetic narrative.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Require the default run to finish with zero residue, and run component verifies separately through the aggregate suite. When a human authorizes the live option, confirm exactly the bounded model leg changes and no brain, soulfile, channel, or production flag is touched.
    Related concepts. See the dark build, the organ map, and the full verify suite.

    scripts/fixtures/generate-synthetic-day.mjs fixture

    What it is. A rehearsal-data generator that creates a plausible day of episodes, intentions, and calendar-shaped records with explicit synthetic provenance.
    What it contains. Every row carries a shared run identifier, rehearsal and synthetic flags, a governed audience, and rehearsal era. The safe default writes an ignored local JSONL store; an explicit brain target uses the narrow client and must be voided immediately.
    Who reads it and when. Component and end-to-end verifies use it before running loops. Operators may use the bounded brain target only under the dark-build residue rule.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Inspect row shapes and tags, run the fixture verify, then pass the printed run identifier to the voider. Success requires the generator's counts and the voider's residual count to agree.
    Related concepts. See rehearsal rules, day inputs, and the voider.

    What it contains. It reads approved environment-variable names from ignored configuration, creates authenticated REST requests, inserts caller-supplied records without validating their tags, deletes by run identifier, and counts remaining rows. It is not the production memory client or general recall path.
    Who reads it and when. The synthetic-day generator and voider import it for their exceptional brain-target mode. Normal fixture runs never need it.
    How to verify or reproduce it. The caller must validate and rehearsal-tag every row before passing it to this client. Use a scratch or sanctioned tiny rehearsal, delete by the same run identifier, and require zero residual. Never print credentials or service coordinates.
    Related concepts. See the Brain, residue rules, and credential scope.

    Related concepts. See orientation and birth status.

Run identifiers must use the rehearsal prefix and resolve inside the rehearsal root; missing or invalid identifiers are usage errors, not broad deletion.

    What it contains. It owns one long-lived process per selected model, sends stream-formatted turns, accumulates partial assistant events, emits complete sentences as they arrive, and records timing and session identifiers for engineering telemetry. A FIFO queue prevents overlapping turns. A true interrupt cancels the active request so barge-in frees the next turn, while a watchdog rejects silence or failure rather than returning an empty reply. Warm-up, shutdown, process errors, malformed events, and queued cancellation have explicit paths.
    Who reads it and when. The streaming voice test server creates it during a human-started audio session. Production voice does not import this test persona as identity or memory.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Use the voice harness with test text to check warm-up, sentence boundaries, queued turns, interruption, timeout, and clean shutdown. Review only gitignored engineering telemetry and confirm no audio bytes, soulfile writes, or brain episodes are created.
    Related concepts. See the voice stack, Testweaver, and the streaming harness.

    How to verify or reproduce it. Install from the lock in a clean test workspace and confirm no unexpected dependency drift. Review integrity and license changes in diffs.
    Related concepts. See voice transport and code licensing.

    What it contains. Barge-in cancels active mind and playback work. It records text and timing telemetry, never audio bytes, in ignored logs and labels the active scratch-brain profile when one is deliberately selected.     Atlas: the verify suite

    TLDR

    The verify suite is the repository's fixed rope: each component ships a repeatable check that prints a first-line result and exits nonzero on failure. Most checks are hermetic dark rehearsals using fixtures, temporary directories, or injected dependencies. They prove named invariants, not every live service. The aggregate runner discovers JavaScript verifies automatically; live machine checks remain explicit and out of band.

    What this page covers

    Entries name what each check pins, the boundary of its evidence, and how it avoids unauthorized side effects. Short component verifies point back to the code they exercise. Larger checks cover cross-file invariants: fleet isolation, dump safety, memory scoping, restore metadata, site release rules, and complete night wiring. A green result is useful only for the exact contract the check actually runs.

    File entries

    scripts/verify/run-all.mjs active-code

    What it is. The aggregate dark-verify runner and standard repository health command.
    What it contains. It discovers every JavaScript file whose name begins with the verify prefix, runs them in sorted order with the current Node executable, retains each child's first output line, and prints a compact pass/fail table plus an all-pass summary. It does not discover the PowerShell live task-import check.
    Who reads it and when. Builders and operators run it after a coherent change set and inside the repository recovery drill. Rerun a failing child directly for its remaining detail.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Add a temporary failing fixture in an isolated copy to prove nonzero propagation, then remove it. Keep every child verify's first line stable and actionable.
    Related concepts. See the dark build, verification cadence, and site verification.

    scripts/verify/task-import-test.ps1 described-not-shown

    What it is. The out-of-band Windows task import-and-remove rehearsal used only at arming.
    What it contains. It converts tracked task definitions to the encoding required by the scheduler, registers each under a temporary test name, confirms disabled state, then removes it. Coordinates are withheld.
    Who reads it and when. An operator runs it on the intended host; the aggregate JavaScript suite does not.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Require every temporary task to register disabled and require cleanup even after failure. Inspect the host privately for residue.
    Related concepts. See scheduled operations and task definitions.

    What it is. The hermetic command-contract check for the brain A/B runner.

    Who reads it and when. The aggregate suite runs it before any lab experiment.
    How to verify or reproduce it. A named live profile must remain harmless in dry-run, while missing or malformed candidate input must fail with usage status.
    Related concepts. See A/B testing and the runner.

No database is contacted.
    Who reads it and when. The aggregate suite runs it whenever fleet code or schema conventions change. Lab operators use it before a real scratch operation.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Keep its synthetic DDL representative of every construct used by canonical brain DDL. A new migration feature needs a pinned case before live propagation.
    Related concepts. See brain fleets, profile guards, and SQL generation.

    Next: Atlas: edge functions →

    Atlas: edge functions

    TLDR

    Edge functions are the guarded doors around remote memory. One interface serves general Open Brain capture and search, another governs reusable agent lessons, recall-scoped applies Edgeweaver's provenance and audience walls, embed-backfill repairs missing vectors, and sql-migrate is a powerful operator-only schema tool. Reviewed mirrors live beside deployment sources so code can be audited without publishing service coordinates or credentials.

    What this page covers

    The deployable functions live under the Supabase source tree. Three smaller files under the scripts tree are byte-matched review mirrors of deployed functions at this snapshot; recall mirror equality is also pinned by verification. Dependency manifests make larger functions reproducible. A shared access-key name is not the whole policy: each entry explains whether the door is general operator tooling, governed agent memory, or the narrower consumer-scoped recall path.

    File entries

    scripts/edge-functions/embed-backfill.ts archive

    What it is. The reviewed repository mirror of the deployed missing-embedding backfill function.
    What it contains. It matches the deployable source byte for byte at this snapshot: select rows without vectors, request embeddings in batches, update rows, and report remaining work. Coordinates and keys stay outside Git.
    Who reads it and when. Reviewers inspect it with ingestion changes; deployment uses the Supabase-tree copy.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Compare bytes with the deployable file and run the private batch to zero remaining rows, checking errors without exposing content.
    Related concepts. See semantic memory and the deployed source.

    scripts/edge-functions/recall-scoped.ts archive

    What it is. The reviewed mirror of the deployable Edgeweaver recall-scoping wall.
    What it contains. It carries the same embedding, semantic match, audience, provenance, and fail-closed filtering logic as the deployed copy. It stores no credential values.
    Who reads it and when. Memory reviewers use it beside conventions; runtime deployment uses the Supabase-tree copy.
    How to verify or reproduce it. The recall-scoping verify requires byte equality and exercises unlabeled, pre-birth, audience, library, fiction, interpretation, and experienced fixtures.
    Related concepts. See recall policy and the deployed wrapper.

    scripts/edge-functions/sql-migrate.ts archive

    What it is. The reviewed mirror of the guarded schema-migration edge function.
    What it contains. It accepts an authenticated SQL script, executes it as one operator transaction context, returns bounded status, and closes its database client. It is powerful operator tooling, not ordinary runtime behavior.
    Who reads it and when. Schema reviewers inspect it before a governed migration; deployment uses the matching Supabase-tree copy.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Compare it bytewise with the deployable source and test only against an approved disposable schema before any live migration.
    Related concepts. See change authority and the deployed source.

    supabase/functions/agent-memory-api/deno.json schema-data

    What it is. The import map that pins the agent-memory function's runtime libraries.
    What it contains. It maps validation, HTTP routing, and database-client package names to explicit versions, making deployment resolution reviewable.
    Who reads it and when. The edge runtime and maintainers read it whenever the agent-memory API builds.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Reproduce dependency resolution in the supported runtime and review every version change with the function tests and upstream licenses.
    Related concepts. See governed lessons and the API source.

    supabase/functions/agent-memory-api/index.ts active-code

    What it is. The governed API for reusable agent memories: recall, writeback, usage traces, review, and audit around the sidecar lesson store. It is distinct from ordinary thought capture.
    What it contains. It validates versioned request bodies, scope, runtime, channel, memory payload, review action, and usage reports. Recall embeds a query, filters and ranks eligible rows, returns policy flags, and records a trace. Writeback derives one or more memory rows, detects only bounded unsafe shapes through unsafeReasons, such as key-like strings, large code blocks, and raw-transcript-like input; it does not establish general instruction safety. It fingerprints records and defaults agent-written lessons to evidence with confirmation pending rather than instruction authority. Review routes can confirm, restrict, reject, stale, or edit records while updating audit history. Access is guarded by the configured brain key; credentials and service coordinates are environment-only.
    Who reads it and when. Approved agent-memory clients call it during recall and post-task writeback. Alan or an authorized review surface handles pending lessons; operators inspect audits during incidents.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Exercise schema rejection, authentication, scoped recall, trust-default writeback, duplicate fingerprints, bounded unsafe-shape refusal, usage marking, every review transition, and audit events against a disposable database. Confirm no pending lesson becomes instruction-grade without review.
    Related concepts. See lessons and trust defaults, confirmation, and scope.

    supabase/functions/embed-backfill/index.ts active-code

    What it is. The deployed batch worker that gives semantic vectors to thought rows inserted without embeddings.
    What it contains. It selects a bounded batch of missing rows, sends truncated content to the configured embedding service, patches successful vectors in small parallel groups, counts remaining work, and returns bounded error summaries. Privileged database and vendor credentials come only from the edge environment.
    Who reads it and when. An operator invokes it after bulk or direct ingestion until the missing count reaches zero. Normal recall benefits from the result but does not call this maintenance function.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Run on a small approved batch, compare embedded and remaining counts, inspect errors privately, repeat to zero, and confirm already embedded rows are never selected.
    Related concepts. See semantic recall, library ingestion, and the review mirror.

    supabase/functions/open-brain-mcp/deno.json schema-data

    What it is. The import map for the Open Brain MCP edge function.
    What it contains. It pins the MCP transport, protocol SDK, HTTP framework, validation library, and database client to explicit versions.
    Who reads it and when. The edge runtime resolves it at build and deployment; maintainers review dependency updates.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Resolve in the supported runtime, run the function's integration checks, and inspect upstream license and security changes before updating pins.
    Related concepts. See Open Brain and the MCP source.

    supabase/functions/open-brain-mcp/index.ts active-code

    What it is. The general Open Brain MCP server for external clients to capture, search, fetch, list, and summarize thoughts. It is not the narrower Edgeweaver consumer-recall wall.
    What it contains. It builds an authenticated MCP server over streamable HTTP, generates embeddings, extracts metadata for capture, and registers read and write tools with protocol annotations. Search and fetch produce citation-shaped results; list and statistics expose bounded summaries; capture writes a thought with generated embedding and structured metadata. A configurable citation base affects links, while database, embedding, and access credentials remain in the edge environment. Because these tools serve broader owner workflows, their general search behavior must not be mistaken for the provenance and audience policy applied to a being's episodic or study recall.
    Who reads it and when. Alan and approved external AI clients use the MCP interface for Open Brain workflows. Edgeweaver runtime consumers should call the scoped wrapper appropriate to their role.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Test authentication, every tool schema, embedding and metadata failures, bounded result shapes, citation construction, read-only annotations, and capture persistence in a disposable project. Separately prove the runtime cannot bypass recall-scoped through credential assignment.
    Related concepts. See brain interfaces, credential separation, and scoped recall.

    supabase/functions/recall-scoped/index.ts active-code

    What it is. The deployable enforcement point that turns semantic memory search into consumer-safe recall by applying both provenance class and audience scope before results leave the brain.
    What it contains. It authenticates the caller, requires a query, accepts a consumer value, obtains a query embedding, overfetches semantic candidates, loads their source and metadata, derives experienced, interpretation, fiction, or library class, and applies the consumer allowlist plus audience algebra. Only the literal consumer value study receives the study policy; every other value currently falls through to the episodic policy. Unlabeled rows fail closed; governed pre-birth rows default to the parent scope rather than public. Results retain useful provenance and similarity while content is bounded.
    Who reads it and when. Waking, voice, study, and other being-facing recall clients call it with an explicit audience scope. Operators review its policy with memory conventions before deployment.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Run the offline scoping verifier across every class and scope, require mirror equality, test authentication and upstream failures in a disposable deployment, and confirm no raw candidate is returned before both filters pass.
    Related concepts. See the one recall door, audience algebra, and the review mirror.

    supabase/functions/sql-migrate/index.ts active-code

    What it is. The deployable guarded DDL runner for reviewed multi-statement schema migrations.
    What it contains. It requires the configured brain access key, validates that the request contains SQL text, opens one direct database client with prepared statements disabled for script execution, runs the supplied text, returns a bounded statement or error result, and always closes the client. It contains no migration policy by itself.
    Who reads it and when. Only an operator uses it for an approved migration when the normal deployment path needs a database-level change. Runtime agents must not receive its credential.
    How to verify or reproduce it. First exercise the matching SQL against a disposable schema, confirm unauthorized and malformed requests fail, inspect transaction behavior, and compare the reviewed mirror with this source before live use.
    Related concepts. See change control, schema evolution, and the review mirror.

    Atlas: tasks/

    TLDR

    These are Windows Task Scheduler definitions for the future operational rhythms: a fallback heartbeat, the night cycle, and the weekly index. Every definition is tracked for review but ships disabled and unregistered. Exact schedules, task coordinates, machine paths, and hosting details are withheld. Static verification proves safe defaults; a human-run import-and-remove rehearsal proves host compatibility before arming.

    What this page covers

    Each XML file describes a trigger, wake behavior, execution command, and disabled settings. They are configuration schemas, not evidence that any job is running. The common safety pattern is more important than the hidden coordinate: an accidental import remains disabled, the host may wake for an enabled future job, and registration happens only after the hosting gate and the associated developmental phase close.

    File entries

    tasks/edgeweaver-heartbeat.xml schema-data

    What it is. The disabled definition for a fallback heartbeat wake when event-driven contact is unavailable.

    Who reads it and when. An operator imports it only after the body and hosting gates close; static verification reads it now.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Require well-formed XML, a trigger, wake enabled, task disabled, and the expected wake-command shape, then use the private import-and-remove rehearsal.
    Related concepts. See proactive attention, scheduling, and waking policy.

    How to verify or reproduce it. Check XML structure, disabled state, wake capability, trigger class, and command shape, followed by the self-cleaning host rehearsal before arming.
    Related concepts. See night metabolism, coherence, and the orchestrator.

    tasks/edgeweaver-weekly-index.xml schema-data

    What it is. The disabled definition for the weekly rebuild, review digest, and boundary-registry maintenance job.
    What it contains. It declares a weekly trigger, wake behavior, chained command shape, and disabled settings, while this site withholds its operational coordinate.
    Who reads it and when. An operator registers it only after the same hosting and phase gates as the night task.

    What this page covers

    These files are text-in and text-out organs beneath the larger ears-and-mouth testbed. The backend can use the existing command-line subscription path or a deterministic test implementation; the raw SDK option remains deliberately unwired. Prompt assembly accepts an injected frozen identity prefix without reading or editing soulfiles itself. Mind-server currently awaits recall, backend completion, and writeback in order; streaming and barge-in live in the separate test-mode harness.

    File entries

    voice/claude-backend.mjs active-code

    What it is. The pluggable model-backend layer used by the mind-server seam and voice tests.
    What it contains. It resolves a safe command-line executable, starts a subscription-backed one-turn process without a shell, parses structured events into text and timing metadata, and exposes a deterministic backend for repeatable tests. The raw SDK branch intentionally refuses because its credit and latency gate is not closed.
    Who reads it and when. Mind-server callers choose a backend explicitly or accept the current subscription default. Dark verifies choose the deterministic implementation; operators control executable and credentials outside Git.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Test executable resolution, structured success, process failure, malformed output, deterministic response, and the refusing raw path. Do not call buffered one-turn output token streaming.
    Related concepts. See the Voice Stack, mind-server, and the streaming test mind.

    voice/mind-server.mjs active-code

    What it is. The invariant text-turn organ that joins recalled context, prompt assembly, a chosen model backend, and memory writeback behind one interface. It is not itself the microphone or speaker server.
    What it contains. A caller injects backend, recall, writeback, soul prefix, and generation. For each turn the module awaits recall, assembles a stable system prefix and per-turn message, awaits the backend result, constructs a voice-channel episode with audience, rehearsal, run, timing, backend, timestamp, and generation metadata, then awaits the injected writeback before returning. Its episode metadata is hard-coded for rehearsal, so arming live use requires configuration or code changes rather than only live dependencies. Defaults make dark testing possible, including a clearly labeled noncanonical prefix. The current implementation is sequential; speculative mid-utterance recall and token streaming belong to surrounding future or test harnesses rather than this function.
    Who reads it and when. Voice adapters and brain-lab experiments call it. The deterministic verifier injects local dependencies; an armed body first requires configuration or code changes to replace hard-coded rehearsal metadata, then scoped recall, real writeback, and the read-only canonical prefix.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Use the mind-server verify to assert prefix order, recall placement, response text, one rehearsal write, metadata, generation stamp, and zero local residue. Separately benchmark the selected backend without confusing latency evidence with arming.
    Related concepts. See the full voice cascade, scoped recall, and canonical identity custody.

    voice/prompt-assembly.mjs described-not-shown

    What it is. The pure helper that places identity prefix, session context, recalled memory, and user text.
    What it contains. It records governed soulfile order, one cache boundary, system context, and per-turn recall. Protected identity is injected, never stored.
    Who reads it and when. Mind-server calls it each turn; tests use the labeled noncanonical placeholder only.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Assert order, one cache boundary, stable prefix, recall placement, and no canonical soul content.
    Related concepts. See the Soul, prompt caching, and mind-server.

    Atlas: the gitignored tiers

    TLDR

    Ignored does not mean unimportant. It means Git must not copy that local material into repository history. Edgeweaver ignores secret values, live operational state, source corpus bytes, rehearsal telemetry, installed dependencies, tool caches, and machine noise for different reasons. This page describes each governed shape and its recovery rule without revealing contents, coordinates, account topology, or protected identity material.

    What this page covers

    Git normally records tracked files so a clone can reproduce the project. An ignore rule tells Git to leave matching local files out of that shared history. Some ignored material is reproducible, such as installed packages. Some is operational and losable, such as a cache. Some is essential but must be recovered through a separate human-governed process, such as credentials. The category determines the recovery rule.

    There are no tracked-file anchors on this page because the files themselves are intentionally outside the tracked set. Instead, the sections name stable tiers and point to the committed templates, scripts, and policies that define safe shapes. The site never derives this page by listing private local contents.

    The ignored tiers

    Secrets and local environment

    Files such as .env.local, other environment variants, and machine-local settings hold values that authorize services or select local resources. Only variable names and purposes belong in tracked documentation. Values never belong in Git, the Brain, logs, artifacts, search, or this site. Recovery uses the separately governed secret-backup procedure; rotation replaces compromised values rather than editing history.

    Operational state

    state/ holds daemon memory such as disabled and armed flags, interlocutor scope, budgets, rehearsal stores, write-ahead records, coherence snapshots, and local verification workspaces. This is not canonical identity. Committed templates define expected schemas, initializers rebuild safe defaults, and component verifies use isolated subdirectories. A write-ahead backlog receives special recovery treatment because it may represent intended writes not yet accepted by the Brain.

    Corpus inputs and staging outputs

    corpus/ contains bulky downloads, private source readings, conversation-export inputs, extracted text, and parser-generated staging data. Rights differ by source: one corpus may permit redistribution while another is a private gift, so the folder-level ignore rule is not a blanket license. Tracked fetchers, parsers, provenance conventions, and source records explain reproduction where lawful. Protected or private inputs are reviewed locally and are never copied into the website.

    Logs and rehearsal telemetry

    logs/ may hold dark-run summaries, A/B transcripts, voice text and timing telemetry, and failure diagnostics. Rehearsal logs are evidence for an operator, not memory or identity, and may contain user text. They remain local, use bounded retention, and must be inspected before any excerpt is shared. Voice test policy stores no audio bytes. Public release evidence records pass or fail and sanitized hashes, not private transcript content.

    Protected soul-source machine material

    Selected machine-readable files under the Genesis soul-source workspace are ignored. Their existence and ceremony role may be named, but their contents and structure remain governed under the pre-A3 redaction tier. They are not canonical identity: canonical identity exists only in the being's own soul repository. Reproduction means following the private harvest and ceremony process, never copying another child's source material.

    Dependencies, caches, and tool state

    node_modules/, Python bytecode caches, deployment-tool links, and Supabase local scratch state are derived machine material. Lockfiles, package manifests, source, and platform configuration are tracked; the bulky installed result is rebuilt. These directories must not be treated as authority, and deleting a cache is not the same as deleting memory, state backlog, or a secret.

    Operating-system noise

    Desktop metadata and thumbnail caches describe the workstation, not Edgeweaver. Ignore rules keep them from creating meaningless diffs or leaking machine detail. They need no backup and can be recreated by the operating system.

    How to reason about an ignored file

    1. Ask why it is ignored. Secret, private source, operational state, derived dependency, cache, and noise are different risk classes.
    2. Find the tracked shape. Look for a template, schema, parser, initializer, runbook, or names-only policy that explains how the file is created and validated.
    3. Choose the right recovery. Rebuild derived material, replay governed backlog, restore private source under its rights, or use the human secret ceremony. Never invent missing values.
    4. Keep proof sanitized. Record that a check passed, which governed class was involved, and where the tracked procedure lives. Do not paste the ignored contents.

    For the repository-wide view, return to the Repo Atlas. For the walls between Git, state, credentials, memory, and soul repositories, read segmentation. For recovery responsibilities, read backups and disaster recovery.

    Atlas: site/ (this website)

    TLDR

    This website is hand-authored static HTML with deterministic generation around it. Authors own each page's main content; shared partials, metadata, and the builder produce navigation, local search, continuation cards, Atlas coverage, and two single-file editions. The deployment is public with no gate; safety comes from publishing no secrets or protected material. Generated outputs are committed evidence, never the source of truth.

    What this page covers

    The entries distinguish authored contract and configuration from executable build code and generated search data. They also explain which tracked website paths deliberately do not receive individual Atlas anchors. That exception keeps this self-documenting site from creating dozens of circular entries while still giving every excluded class a named home, a verification rule, and a searchable explanation.

    File entries

    scripts/site/build-site.mjs active-code

    What it is. The deterministic assembler for shared page chrome, local search, Atlas manifest, and the full and lite single-file editions. It is the only writer for marked generated regions and outputs.
    What it contains. It validates navigation hubs, page metadata, audiences, and reading tracks; fills head, contextual navigation, breadcrumbs, search dialog, local find fallback, page tables of contents, continuation cards, and footer markers; extracts authored main content into normalized search records; scrapes file anchors into the manifest; and builds self-contained artifact documents with one main landmark and page articles. The generated search index and artifacts share those builder in-memory records; artifacts do not read generated JavaScript. Lite output omits detailed Atlas pages while adding one distinct map row for every individually mapped tracked path; named exclusion classes cover the remaining tracked paths. Exact path mappings override broad exclusion classes. Check mode computes all outputs in memory and reports stale files without writing.
    Who reads it and when. Luna runs it under a writer freeze after authors stop. Authors edit only main content and shared owners edit partials or metadata; end users consume its outputs.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Run check mode for freshness, regenerate once under freeze, rerun check, compare byte identity, and execute default, live-drift, redaction, and release verification as required. Never resolve coverage from Git inside the builder itself.
    Related concepts. See how the site is made, Repository 101, and the authoring contract.

    site/.gitignore schema-data

    What it is. The site-local ignore rules for deployment-tool state and environment files.
    What it contains. It excludes the local project-link directory and every site-level environment file, preventing machine metadata and passwords from becoming tracked website source.
    Who reads it and when. Git applies it during local deployment work; operators review it before adding configuration.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Use Git's ignore explanation on representative local files and confirm no ignored value appears in tracked status or Atlas output.
    Related concepts. See secret separation and ignored tiers.

    site/.vercelignore schema-data

    What it is. The deployment-upload exclusion list for material that Vercel does not need to serve.
    What it contains. It omits authoring sources, artifact editions, the handoff README, and repository-only metadata from uploads. Public output remains deployable.
    Who reads it and when. The deployment client reads it during a manual site release; maintainers review changes with the build layout.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Inspect the upload plan privately; smoke-test a page, asset, nested Atlas route, and missing route on the live deployment.
    Related concepts. See editions and manual release.

    site/README.md runbook

    What it is. The maintenance guide that becomes the explainer site's operational handoff only after Luna updates it.
    What it contains. After Luna updates it, it records the current execution resume point, build and verification commands, preview options, source and generated layout, public-posture handling, editorial rules, and milestone ledger. It is a status aid for builders, not the public conceptual guide or design authority.
    Who reads it and when. The next coding agent reads it as the handoff after Luna's update; until then, its resume and milestone prose is not current handoff status. A newcomer should use the Reading Guide for repository vocabulary.
    How to verify or reproduce it. After Luna updates it, reconcile its commands, generated-output list, active phase, and milestone state with the plan and actual scripts. Remove stale claims rather than treating prose as automatic status.
    Related concepts. See How to read this site, project status, and authoring rules.

    site/package.json schema-data

    What it is. The minimal Node package marker for the framework-less static site.
    What it contains. It names a private package and selects module semantics. No dependencies or scripts exist; commands live in the site README.
    Who reads it and when. Node and the deployment platform use it to interpret JavaScript modules. Maintainers read it when adding tooling.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Parse it as JSON, confirm private status and module mode, and avoid inventing an install or test step that the manifest does not define.
    Related concepts. See the dependency-free site and build commands.

    site/public/assets/search-index.js generated

    What it is. The generated, network-free search dataset for every web page.
    What it contains. It carries a release identifier and normalized heading and file records: destination, audience, register, badges, path, and text. It stores no queries or analytics.
    Who reads it and when. Browser search loads it. Artifacts receive the builder's shared in-memory records instead; they do not read this generated JavaScript. Authors never edit it.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Rebuild under freeze; parse the payload, check destinations and redaction, and test exact-path ranking.
    Related concepts. See local search, generated outputs, and the builder.

    site/public/assets/LICENSE-CODE.txt generated

    What it is. The distributable MIT notice for the site's HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and build code.
    What it contains. The complete permission, attribution, warranty, and liability text copied from the repository's code-license decision.
    Who reads it and when. A recipient reads it before copying code from the deployed site; the artifact and about page carry the same licensing boundary.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Compare this asset byte-for-byte with the approved code notice before a release and confirm it is present in the deployed public asset set.
    Related concepts. See license and attribution and the site handoff.

    site/src/AUTHORING.md authority

    What it is. The binding editorial and markup contract for every authored byte in the explainer. The higher design plan governs it when a conflict is discovered.
    What it contains. It defines secret, probe, identity, people, status, canonical-soul, and operational redaction rules; page mechanics and relative links; navigation metadata; deterministic search; progressive enhancement and reading lens behavior; exact Atlas article fields, badges, and depth bands; accessibility requirements for controls, tables, diagrams, anchors, mobile, print, and reduced motion; diagram conventions; and the allowed targeted self-check. It also separates machine-owned marker regions from author-owned main content and forbids authors from racing the builder.
    Who reads it and when. Every site author and reviewer reads it fully before editing. Luna owns shared implementation, while Atlas authors follow its frozen entry contract inside assigned pages.
    How to verify or reproduce it. The release verifier automates structural portions, but editorial review must still inspect truth, redaction, plain-language quality, and authority conflicts. Update the contract and verifier together when a rule becomes mechanical, then regenerate only under the integration freeze.
    Related concepts. See editorial honesty, authority order, and site method.

    site/src/allowed-domains.txt schema-data

    What it is. The small editorial allowlist for external hyperlinks in site pages.
    What it contains. It lists approved host domains only, one per line. It is not a network firewall, runtime service list, or permission to load remote assets.
    Who reads it and when. The site verifier reads it; authors consult it before adding a rare external citation.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Confirm every external anchor is secure and on the list, every remote asset or fetch remains forbidden, and each domain is still necessary.
    Related concepts. See attribution and network boundaries.

    site/src/atlas-map.json schema-data

    What it is. The coverage-routing table that assigns every individually mapped repository path to one Atlas page and names exclusion classes for the remaining tracked paths.
    What it contains. It defines exact paths and longest-prefix destinations plus named exclusions for the broad site-page surface and selected generated outputs. The lite map has one row for every individually mapped path, while these named exclusions cover the remaining tracked paths. An exact mapped file, such as the generated search index, overrides a broad excluded prefix. Notes record the page responsible for explaining each exception.
    Who reads it and when. The builder uses it when emitting the committed manifest; live-drift verification compares its policy with tracked files. Atlas authors use it to respect ownership, never to derive content.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Run the read-only tracked-path comparison after additions or renames. Require zero unmapped paths, no wrong-page anchors, no orphaned manifest entries, and a documented home for every exclusion.
    Related concepts. See the Repo Atlas, tracked paths, and this coverage rule.

    site/src/nav.json schema-data

    What it is. The single metadata source for page order, five hubs, reading tracks, titles, snapshot, release identifier, search classification, and audiences.
    What it contains. Every page record supplies slug, title, milestone, hub, subsection, kind, summary, and one or more approved audiences. Hub definitions name their landing pages, while three explicit tracks define continuation cards without inferred state.
    Who reads it and when. The builder validates and renders it into shared navigation, breadcrumbs, search records, artifact contents, and continuation links. Authors consult it but do not change slugs casually.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Require exactly five valid hubs, unique slugs, known kinds and audiences, complete metadata, nonrepeating valid tracks, and a deliberate release identifier before shipping. Then test every generated destination.
    Related concepts. See reading paths, site structure, and the renderer.

    site/src/partials/footer.html active-code

    What it is. The shared closing template inserted after every authored main.
    What it contains. It holds generated continuation-card placement, the village-layer banner, documentation license and attribution, snapshot, and release identifier.
    Who reads it and when. The builder reads it for web pages; authors see its output but do not edit marker regions.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Regenerate and confirm every page has one footer, correct local links, current release metadata, and required attribution in both artifacts.
    Related concepts. See license and editions and the builder.

    site/src/partials/head.html active-code

    What it is. The shared document-head template for every static page.
    What it contains. It declares encoding, viewport, no-index metadata, release metadata, a page title, local stylesheet, generated search data, and enhancement script using the page's relative root.
    Who reads it and when. The builder inserts it; browsers load the resulting local resources.
    How to verify or reproduce it. Check every page has one resolved title and root-correct local asset paths under file, static HTTP, and nested Atlas modes.

    site/src/partials/nav.html active-code

    What it is. The shared shell for controls, search, contextual navigation, breadcrumbs, reading column, and on-page rail.
    What it contains. It provides accessible labels and placeholders for hub links, mobile controls, search, reading detail, theme, snapshot, no-JS help, TOCs, and the page main boundary.
    Who reads it and when. The builder fills it for every page; browser JavaScript progressively enhances its controls.

    site/vercel.json schema-data

    What it is. The static deployment configuration for the public site project.

    Who reads it and when. The deployment platform reads it during a manual release; operators review it with the cache and header policy.

    Tracked exclusion classes

    site/public/: site-pages

    The authored HTML pages, shared stylesheet, and browser enhancement script are tracked and served, but they do not each receive a circular file entry. Their concepts are the site itself; their shared authoring, build, search, and verification rules are documented on this page. The exact-mapped generated search index is the deliberate exception and has its own entry above.

    Generated editions and manifest

    The committed full artifact, lite artifact, and Atlas manifest are deterministic builder outputs. They carry no individual file-* anchors because editing them directly would reverse source and output. The builder entry explains reproduction; freshness and release verification prove that each generated byte matches authored pages, metadata, partials, and styles.
